source_ref: Class 10 Political Science (Democratic Politics II, CBSE 2025-26) - original one-line definitions and facts.

items.definition: An arrangement in which leaders recognised regional differences and cultural diversities and amended the constitution four times between 1970 and 1993.
A policy of refusing to share power and giving primacy to one community, as in Sri Lanka's Sinhala Only Act of 1956.
A third kind of Belgian government, elected by people belonging to one language group, responsible for culture, education and language.
Sharing of power among the legislature, executive and judiciary, each checking the others.
Sharing of power among governments at different levels: union, state and local.
A practical argument that sharing power reduces the possibility of conflict between social groups and ensures political stability.
The argument that power sharing is valuable in itself because people have a right to be consulted on how they are governed.
A system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and various constituent units of the country.
A federation in which independent states join together to form a bigger unit, as in the USA, Australia and Switzerland.
A federation in which a large country divides power between the constituent states and the national government, as in India, Spain and Belgium.
The list of subjects of national importance on which only the central government may legislate, such as defence and foreign affairs.
The list of subjects of state and local importance on which only the state government may legislate, such as police and agriculture.
The list of subjects of common interest on which both the union and state governments may legislate, such as education and marriage.
The transfer of power from central and state governments to local government bodies.
India's system of rural local self-government, constitutionally mandated by the 73rd Amendment of 1992.
The number of females per one thousand males in a population.
A society in which men are given more power and status than women, including within the family.
Politics that treats religion as the basis of social community and uses religious difference to gain political advantage.
A state with no official religion, which gives freedom to practise any religion and intervenes to ensure equal treatment.
A group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government, agreeing on some policies and programmes.
A party that is not in power and whose role is to criticise the government and hold it accountable.
A system in which only one party is allowed to rule, as in China, with no free competition for power.
A system in which power usually changes between two main parties, as in the United Kingdom and the United States.
A system in which several parties compete for power and more than two have a serious chance, as in India.
A government formed by two or more parties joining together when no single party gets a clear majority.
A government that is answerable to the people and follows procedures that can be examined and questioned.
A government that is elected by the people and is therefore accepted and recognised as their own.
